title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
## Private landlords' rights, responsibilities and the law
If you own land or a building and rent it to a tenant, you are considered a landlord.
Your main rights and responsibilities as a landlord come from:
Landlord and tenant law
The lease or tenancy agreement (written or spoken) you have with your tenant
Landlord and tenant law
Residential tenancies legislation outlines most landlord’s rights and obligations. You can read a consolidated version of the Residential Tenancies Act 2004 on the Law Reform Commission's website.
Leases and tenancy agreements
Leases or other tenancy agreements cannot take away from your landlord or tenant rights and responsibilities in the legislation.
However, you and your tenant can agree on things that are not covered by legislation in a lease or tenancy agreement, for example, who pays for the utility bills.

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Approved housing body landlords and the law
Approved housing bodies (AHBs) are covered by residential tenancies legislation. AHB landlords have most of the same rights and responsibilities as private landlords.
However, there are some differences, including the rules on rent reviews , minimum standards and a landlord’s right to end a tenancy .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Student-specific accommodation landlords and the law
Student-specific accommodation (SSA) is housing that is:
Built or designated for students
Used solely to provide residential accommodation to students during the academic term
Landlords and tenants in student-specific accommodation are protected in residential tenancies legislation. This means that they have most of the same rights as private landlords and tenants. However, there are some differences:
Tenants in student-specific accommodation do not have security of tenure
Landlords may be able to access communal areas without the permission of the tenants
Tenancy or licence arrangements in student-specific accommodation should not be more than 41 weeks .
Tenants in student-specific accommodation only need to give you 28 days’ notice when they end their tenancy. You must give them more notice when ending their tenancy .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
## Your rights as a landlord
As a landlord, you have the right to:
Set the rent
Get the correct rent on the date it is due
Get any charges associated with the property (this means taxes and duties or payments)
Terminate a tenancy during the first 6 months without giving a reason
Terminate a tenancy at a later stage in certain circumstances
Be told about who lives at the property (this does not include overnight visitors or short stays)
Be told about any repairs needed
Be given reasonable access to the property to carry out repairs
Carry out routine inspections at a mutually agreed time. Repairs or inspections should be arranged in advance with your tenant, unless there is an emergency. If you are selling the property, your tenant must allow you access for viewings, but this must be arranged with them beforehand.
Refer disputes to the RTB – but only if you have registered the tenancy

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
## Your responsibilities as a landlord
As a landlord, you must:
Register the tenancy every year with the RTB and update them about any changes to the tenancy, such as a change in rent
Give your tenant a rent book or statement of rent paid
Make sure that the property meets certain minimum standards . The standards for food preparation, storage and laundry purposes do not apply to AHBs.
Repair and maintain the inside of the property to the standard it was in at the start of the tenancy
Repair and maintain the structure of the property
Provide a Building Energy Rating (BER) for the property
Pay your tenants back for any repairs they make which are your responsibility
Insure the property. If it is impossible to get insurance, or if the cost is unreasonable, this does not apply.

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Advertising accommodation for sexual
activity
You cannot offer or advertise accommodation in exchange for sexual activity. This is a criminal offence that applies to tenancies and licence arrangements and can result in Class A fine of up to €5,000. This is set out in the Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Deposits
You cannot ask for upfront payments of more than 2 month’s rent when renting out a property. This includes a deposit of a month’s rent and one month’s rent in advance.
Students in student-specific tenancies can opt-out of this restriction and pay a larger upfront payment if they want. However, this opt-out is only allowed if the student is paying rent and tuition to the same provider, such as a public or private educational provider.
You can only withhold a tenant’s deposit if:
Your tenant has not given you proper notice when ending the tenancy
You have been left with unpaid rent or outstanding bills, for example for electricity or gas
Your tenant has caused damage beyond normal wear and tear

The Residential Tenancies (Amendment) Act 2015 provides for a tenancy deposit protection scheme , where the RTB would manage and hold deposits for tenants and landlords. These provisions are not yet in effect.

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Refusing a tenancy
Landlords cannot discriminate against potential tenants on grounds of gender, civil status, family status, sexual orientation, religion, age, disability, race or membership of the Traveller community.
You cannot discriminate against a tenant or potential tenant because they are getting a Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) , Rent Supplement or any other social welfare payment.
This means that you cannot state when advertising accommodation that HAP or Rent Supplement is not accepted and you cannot refuse to rent accommodation to someone because they are getting a social welfare payment.
The is outlined in the Equal Status Acts , which apply to lettings and accommodation.
Read more on the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission's website .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Ending a tenancy
If you want to end a tenancy, you must serve your tenant with a valid written Notice of Termination and give them the correct amount of notice .
You must send a copy of this Notice of Termination to the RTB. Since 14 September 2026, you have 7 days from the date the tenant is served the notice of termination to send a copy to the RTB.
You can find out more on ending a tenancy the RTB's website .

## What if I break these rules?
Landlords who break their obligations can be dealt with in several ways.
You can be:
Prosecuted
Investigated and sanctioned
Fined

### Criminal prosecution
You can be criminally prosecuted for breaking certain rental rules, such as not registering a tenancy or not complying with a determination order. This can result in:
A criminal conviction
A fine of up to €5,000
Imprisonment for up to 12 months

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Investigation and sanction
The RTB can investigate, caution and sanction you if you break your statutory obligations as a landlord.
The RTB can investigate several issues, such as not registering a tenancy or following the rent increase rules.
Find out exactly what issues the RTB can investigate in our page Reporting an issue to the RTB .
If you are found guilty any of breaking these rules, you can get:
A written caution
A fine of up to €15,000 for each breach
Additional costs up to €15,000 for each breach
The RTB has more information about decisions and sanctions .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Fixed payment fines
Since 14 September 2026, the RTB can issue fixed payment fines if you break certain rental laws, such as:
Not registering a tenancy
Not updating details about a tenancy
Not giving rent setting information at the start of a tenancy
Setting the rent above the rent increase limits
Not notifying the RTB of a rent exemption
Not providing a rent review notice correctly
You can be fined €200 for breaking the rent increase rules and €100 for breaking the registration rules.
You have 28 days from the date of the notice to pay the fine. If you do not to pay the fine during this time, you may be prosecuted.
As well as issuing these fines, the RTB can also prosecute and investigate.
You can find out more about these fines on the RTB’s website .

## Rental income and tax

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Tax issues
Landlords pay tax on rental income.
You can claim certain expenses against your rental income to reduce the amount of tax you pay. For example, you can claim for repairs to the property and management fees.
Revenue has a list if what expenses you are allowed to deduct when paying tax on your rental income.
You declare your rental income in your annual tax return, using either Revenue's myAccount Service or ROS (Revenue Online Service) . Revenue has more information on how you can do this.

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Mortgage interest
You can deduct the interest on mortgages used to purchase, improve or repair rented property when working out your rental income for tax purposes.
You must show that you have registered all tenancies in the property with the RTB. You can deduct 100% of the interest on these mortgages.
Interest is treated as accruing on a daily basis and the date the loan was taken out is not relevant. Interest can only be deducted during the period in which the property is let.

### Rent a room relief
If you rent out a room or flat in your home , you are exempt from income tax on the amount that your tenant pays you for rent and other services, up to €14,000 in a tax year. This exemption does not apply to income you get from renting your property for short-term lets .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Rental income tax relief
A temporary rental income tax relief was introduced in 2024 to support private landlords. The Residential Premises Rental Income Relief (RPRIR) is available against some rental income at the standard rate of 20% each year. It is from 2024 to 2027 and only applies if you keep the rental property in the rental market for the next 4 years. You can get 20% of:
€3,000 for 2024
€4,000 for 2025
€5,000 for 2026 and 2027
The relief reduces the tax due on rental income by up to €600 in 2024, €800 in 2025, and €1,000 in 2026 and 2027. The relief will be clawed back if you leave the rental market during this time.
Revenue has more information about the Residential Premises Rental Income Relief .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
### Paying tax on rental income, if you are a landlord living abroad
If you are living outside Ireland and renting out a property in Ireland, you still need to declare your rental income to Revenue and pay tax on it. You can do this by:
Getting your tenant to withhold 20% of their gross rent and pay it to Revenue
Use a collection agent to withhold 20% of your tenant’s rent to pay it to Revenue
Read more in our page on tax relief and other issues for people renting .

title: Landlords’ rights and responsibilities
text:
## Private tenancies and receivership
If the mortgage on your property is in arrears and the mortgage lender has appointed a receiver, your tenants must pay the rent to the receiver. However, you remain legally responsible for things such as returning the tenants’ deposits. The receiver may arrange to do repairs.
Read more in the Residential Tenant’s Guide to Receivership (pdf) published by Banking and Payments Federation Ireland.

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## Introduction
Landlords must:
Register residential tenancies with the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) every year
Update the RTB if information about a tenancy changes
The RTB uses this information to keep a public register of tenancies . This register is a list of all private, approved housing body and cost rental tenancies currently registered with the RTB.
There is a separate register for student specific accommodation tenancies .
The register shows the address of the property. It does not show the identity of the landlord or the tenants.

## What tenancies must a landlord register?
Most privately rented properties must be registered with the RTB.
This applies to:
Private landlords
Approved housing bodies (AHBs)
Landlords of student-specific accommodation
Landlords of cost rental homes

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## What tenancies does a landlord not need to register?
These rented properties do not need to be registered with the RTB:
Business lettings – properties used for business purposes
Holiday lettings – short-term lettings for holidays
Former rent-controlled properties or long-occupation lease tenancies – separate legislation applies to these tenancies and they are not covered by residential tenancies legislation
Owner-occupied accommodation – for example, if you rent a room in your landlord's home
Informal family arrangements – properties where the spouse, parent or child of the landlord lives and there is no formal tenancy agreement in writing. However, the legislation does cover formal agreements between family members, for example, where a lease has been signed.
Social housing – housing provided by local authorities
Temporary accommodation for hosting refugees from Ukraine with the Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP)

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## Do I need to register a home I rent out in my back garden?
If you rent out a home in your garden you may need to register the tenancy with the RTB. Some of these tenancies must be registered and others do not. The rules depend on when the home was added and if you got a planning exemption for it.
If the home was in place before 27 July 2026 , it must be registered with the RTB if it is rented out. This applies even if the home is first rented out after 27 July 2026 .
The landlord and tenant are covered by residential tenancies legislation and have certain rights and responsibilities.
If the home was added on or after 27 July 2026 and got a planning exemption , it does not have to be registered with the RTB. To get this planning exemption the garden home must meet specific requirements .

## Do I need to register a home I rent out in my back garden?

In these situations, the person renting the garden home is not a tenant but a licensee. They are in the rented property with the landlord’s consent. This means they have fewer legal protections than a tenant as they are not covered by residential tenancies legislation.
If the home was added from 27 July 2026 and did not get a valid planning exemption , it must be registered with the RTB.
You can find more information about this exemption in our page ‘ Planning permission for altering your home ’ and in the specific regulations . You can contact your local authority if you have any questions.

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## How often must tenancies be registered?
Landlords are responsible for registering tenancies .
Landlords need to register tenancies each year.
New tenancies must be registered by the landlord within a month of the start of the tenancy.
After that, landlords must re-register the tenancy every year that the same tenancy continues. This must be done within a month of the date of when the tenancy first began.
For example, if a new tenancy began on 4 July 2025, the landlord must register the tenancy by 3 August 2025 (within one month of the tenancy start date). If the tenancy continues for the next 12 months, the landlord must register the tenancy again by 3 August 2026, and then every year by 3 August while the tenancy continues.
The RTB will remind landlords when their tenancy is due for annual registration, if they have up-to-date contact information for the landlord.

## What information do I need to register a tenancy?
Private landlords and approved housing bodies must give this information when registering a tenancy:
Property information for the rented home
The address and Eircode
Property type, for example, is it a house or apartment
The floor area
Number of bedrooms
The Building Energy Rating (BER) , if applicable
The local authority area the property is in
Landlord’s information
The landlord’s name, address, date of birth and Personal Public Service number (PPS number)
Company name and Companies Registration Office (CRO) number, if the landlord is a company
The approved housing body (AHB) number, if the landlord is an AHB
Tenancy information
The date the tenancy started
The rent and how often it is paid
Details about the deposit
Any charges that the tenants pay for, such as electricity or gas
The term of the lease if it is a fixed-term lease
If it is a sub-letting

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
### Telling the RTB about changes to rent
If you change the rent, you must tell the RTB.
You must send the completed RTB Notice of Rent Review form (pdf) to your tenant at least 90 days before the new rent begins.
Since 14 September 2026, you will have 7 days from when the tenant is served the notice of rent review to send a copy to the RTB. Previously you had to send it to the tenant and the RTB at the same time.
If you do not follow these rules, the notice is invalid.
You also need to update the RTB tenancy registration record with details of the new rent within a month of the rent changing.
Read more about this in our page on rent increases .

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## How do I know if my tenancy is registered?
You can view the public register to check that your tenancy has been registered.
If you are in student-specific accommodation, you can check the separate register for student specific accommodation tenancies .
The RTB can take action against landlords who do not register tenancies. See ' Penalties for not registering a tenancy with the RTB ' below for more information.
Even if your landlord hasn’t registered your tenancy, you can still use the RTB’s dispute resolution service . Landlords can only use this service if they have registered the tenancy.

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## How much does it cost to register?
The fees for registering a tenancy with the RTB are different depending on the type of tenancy. For example, the fee to register an AHB tenancy is different to the fee to register a private rented tenancy.
There are certain exemptions from annual registration fees, see below.

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
### Registration fees for private, student-specific and cost rental tenancies
The basic fee for registering a private rented, student-specific or cost rental tenancy with the RTB is €40 a year.
This applies if the RTB gets the completed application within a month of the start of the tenancy. There is a late fee of €10 per month for each month that the registration is late.
If you are registering up to 10 tenancies in the same building at the same time, you can pay a combined fee of €170, if you register on time.
You do not have to pay an extra fee for any tenancy changes or further registrations you make within 12 months of registering.

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
### Registration fees for approved housing bodies (AHBs)
The standard fee for registering an AHB tenancy is €20 a year. This rate applies if the tenancy is registered within a month of the start of the tenancy.
There is a late fee of €5 per month for each month that the registration is late.
If you are registering up to 10 AHB tenancies in the same building you can pay a combined fee of €85, if you register them on time.
You do not have to pay an extra fee for any tenancy changes or further registrations you make within 12 months of registering.

### Late fees
If you are late registering a tenancy, late fees apply for each month that the registration is late.

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
### Exemptions from annual registration fees
Before annual registration, tenancies were registered each time a new tenancy began. For example, when new tenants moved in under a new lease. An ongoing tenancy was also re-registered after 6 years. This is known as a ‘ Further Part 4 ’ tenancy.
There is a temporary exemption from annual registration fees for landlords who have ‘Further Part 4’ tenancies. This means they do not have to pay annual registration fees for the time remaining on their ‘Further Part 4’ tenancy. So, if there are 3 years left on a ‘Further Part 4’ tenancy, the landlord does not have to pay annual registration fees for those 3 years. The tenancy must still be registered annually.
This temporary annual registration fee waiver is set out in the Residential Tenancies (Amendment) Act 2021 .
For more information on annual registration and the temporary fee exemption, see the RTB’s website .

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
### Information sharing
The RTB can share information with local authorities, who enforce the regulations on minimum standards and rent books .
It can also share information with the Department of Social Protection and the Revenue Commissioners .

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## How to register a tenancy with the RTB
You can register a tenancy online or by post or email.
You can register a tenancy:
Online using the RTB’s Tenancy Registration Account . You need to set up a registration account to do this, if you do not already have one. The RTB’s website has information about how to do this . If you need to create an online account for an approved housing body (AHB) you should contact AHB@rtb.ie.
By post or email by downloading the RTB 1 Form (pdf) . Complete the form and send it back to the RTB. You can return it by post to the RTB’s address below or email it to registrations@rtb.ie. You should keep a copy of the form and proof of postage.
There is a different process for registering tenancies in student-specific accommodation. See the RTB’s website for information on how to do this.
If you have questions about the registration process, you can email registrations@rtb.ie.

title: Registering a tenancy
text:
## Penalties for not registering a tenancy with the RTB
Landlords who do not register a tenancy can be dealt with in a number of ways.

### Criminal prosecution
Landlords can be criminally prosecuted, which can result in:
A criminal conviction
A fine of up to €5,000
Imprisonment for up to 12 months
An additional penalty of €1,000 for each day the tenancy is not registered
Having to pay the RTB's legal costs

### Investigation and sanction
Alternatively, the RTB can investigate and sanction the landlord. This can result in:
A sanction of up to €15,000
€15,000 in costs for each unregistered tenancy

Since 14 September 2026, the RTB can issue landlords with a fixed payment notice if they break certain rental laws. A landlord can be fined €100 for not registering a tenancy.
A landlord has 28 days from the date of the notice to pay the fine. If the landlord does not to pay the fine, the RTB can investigate or prosecute the landlord,
Read more about these penalties on the RTB’s website .

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
## Rules for ending a tenancy
Landlords must follow certain rules if they want you to leave your rented accommodation.
The rules apply to:
Private landlords
Approved housing bodies
People who let student-specific accommodation
If your landlord wants to end your tenancy, they must:
Serve you with a notice of termination
Give you the correct amount of notice
Send a copy of the notice of termination to the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB)
If your tenancy has lasted less than 6 months, your landlord can ask you to leave without giving you a reason.
If your tenancy has lasted more than 6 months, your landlord must give you a valid reason why they are terminating your tenancy.
The valid reasons are different depending on if your tenancy began:
On or after 1 March 2026

## Valid reasons for ending a tenancy created from 1 March 2026
If your tenancy was created on or after 1 March 2026, you have a tenancy of minimum duration when you have rented for 6 months without getting a notice of termination.
A tenancy of minimum duration runs for 6-year cycles, which means you have security of tenure for 6 years at a time.
Your landlord can only end a tenancy of minimum duration for certain reasons. These reasons depend on how many tenancies your landlord has.
Larger landlords are registered companies, or landlords with 4 or more tenancies.
Smaller landlords are landlords that have 3 or fewer tenancies.
Registered companies are classified as larger landlords, even if they have 3 or less tenancies.

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
### Reasons for larger landlords to end a tenancy of minimum duration
Larger landlords can only end a tenancy of minimum duration if:
The tenants are not meeting their obligations, such as paying rent
The property is no longer suitable, for example, the property is now too small for a family or is not accessible
Larger landlords must follow the correct process when ending a tenancy for these reasons. This includes issuing a valid notice of termination and meeting any other requirements .

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
### Reasons for smaller landlords to end a tenancy of minimum duration
Smaller landlords can only end a tenancy during the 6-year period of a TMD if:
The tenant is not meeting their obligations, such as paying the rent
The property is no longer suitable for the tenant, for example, the property is now too small for a family or is not accessible
The landlord is experiencing hardship, for example, because of a separation, homelessness, bankruptcy or after returning to Ireland from abroad
The landlord needs the property for themselves or an immediate family member to live in. In this situation immediate family members can be, the landlord's spouse, civil partner, child, stepchild, foster child, adopted child, parent, step-parent or parent in-law.
After the 6-year period, smaller landlords can also end a tenancy of minimum duration for these other reasons:
They intend to sell the property
They are substantially refurbishing or renovating the property

## Valid reasons for ending a tenancy created before 1 March 2026
If your tenancy was created before 1 March 2026, your landlord can only end a tenancy after the first 6 months if:
You do not comply with the obligations of the tenancy , for example, by not paying your rent on time
The property is no longer suited to your needs, for example, if it is too small
The landlord intends to sell the property within 9 months. However, this may not apply if the landlord plans to sell 10 or more dwellings in a development within a 6-month period – see ‘Restriction on terminating when selling multiple properties’ below
The landlord needs the property for their own use or for an immediate family member (this only applies to private landlords)
The landlord plans to change the use of the property (for example, convert it from residential use to office use)
The landlord intends to refurbish the property substantially

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
### Additional reasons if your tenancy started before 11 June 2022
If your tenancy was created before 11 June 2022 , your landlord can also terminate your tenancy for any reason at the end of your 6-year, Part 4 tenancy. Your landlord must:
Serve a notice of termination before the end of the 6 years, and
Give a notice period that expires on or after the end of the tenancy
If the tenancy is not ended after 6 years, a new tenancy will begin. This new tenancy will be a tenancy of unlimited duration and this exception will no longer apply.
By June 2028, all Part 4 tenancies will be tenancies of unlimited duration , and the above exception will no longer apply to them. This is because all existing 6-year cycle tenancies will have ended by then.
Your landlord must follow the correct process when ending a tenancy for these reasons.

## Restriction on terminating tenancies when selling multiple properties
A landlord cannot terminate a tenancy of more than 6 months if they intend to sell 10 or more homes in a development within a 6-month period, unless:
They can show that the market value with a sitting tenant is over 20% below the market value with vacant possession, and
Preventing them from terminating the tenancy would be unduly onerous on them or would cause them undue hardship
This provision is often called the ‘ Tyrrelstown amendment’ .

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
## Notice of termination
If your landlord wants you to leave, they must serve you with a valid written notice of termination.
The law sets out the requirements for a valid notice of termination. It must:
Be in writing
Be signed by the landlord, or their authorised agent
Specify the date when the tenancy will end
State that you have the whole 24 hours of the termination date to vacate the property
Specify the date of the notice itself. This is the date the notice is hand delivered, emailed, or left at the tenant's address.
Give the reason for ending the tenancy, if a tenancy has lasted more than 6 months or is a fixed-term tenancy
State that any issue about the validity of the notice or the right of the landlord to serve it must be referred to the RTB within 90 days from getting the notice. (This 90-day timeframe applies unless the tenant is not keeping their obligations.)

### What is a statutory declaration?
A statutory declaration is a signed statement that information is true or accurate. In Ireland, you sign a statutory declaration in the presence of a:
Commissioner for Oaths
Practicing solicitor
Notary public
Peace commissioner
There are more statutory declarations available for joint landlords. You can find these on the RTB’s website .

### Additional rules if your tenancy is ending because a breach of tenant obligations
If your landlord is terminating your tenancy because you have broken your tenant obligations, you must get a written warning notice at least 28 days before the notice of termination is issued.
However, if your behaviour is seriously anti-social your landlord does not have to give you a warning notice. The Notice periods section below has more information on this process.

## Making a complaint about a notice of termination
You can complain to the Residential Tenancies Board if you think:
Your notice of termination is invalid
The reason your landlord gives for ending the tenancy is not allowed

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
### Minor errors in a notice of termination
When dealing with a dispute about a notice of termination, the RTB can overlook a minor error or omission in a notice of termination.
They can do this if the error does not prejudice the notice of termination and the notice would otherwise be valid. This is known as the ‘ slip rule ’.
A ‘remedial notice’ can be issued that fixes the error with the original notice. For more information on remedial notices see the RTB’s website .
Since 14 September 2026, the slip rule also applies to any additional documents you might need for a notice of termination, such as a statutory declaration or statement. This means that minor errors in these documents can also be overlooked and corrected.

## What are the notice periods?
The length of notice required depends on the length of your tenancy.
Length of tenancy Notice that the landlord must give

These notice periods have applied since 6 July 2022, when changes under the Regulation of Providers of Building Works and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2022 took effect.

### Exceptions to required notice periods

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
#### Not keeping your tenant obligations
If you are not keeping your obligations, your landlord must send you a warning notice before they can issue a notice of termination.
The warning notice must outline what obligations have been broken and give you a reasonable amount of time to fix the issue. This warning notice needs to be copied to the RTB.
If you do not resolve the issue, the landlord only needs to give you 28 days’ notice of termination. This applies to all tenancies, regardless of the length of the tenancy.
However, if your behaviour is seriously anti-social or threatens the fabric of the property, the landlord only needs to give you 7 days’ notice and does not have to give you a warning notice.
The Residential Tenancies Act 2004 sets out the type of seriously anti-social behaviour for which a 7-day notice may be allowed.

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
#### Rent arrears
If you haven’t paid your rent, your landlord must send you a rent arrears warning notice before they can issue a notice of termination.
The rent arrears warning notice must state the amount of rent you owe and give you 28 days to pay it. The landlord must send a copy of the rent arrears warning notice to the RTB.
The 28 days you have to pay the rent arrears counts from the date you and the RTB get the warning notice. If your landlord does not send the warning notice to you and the RTB, a notice of termination will not be valid.
If you do not pay the rent arrears in the 28 days, your landlord can then give you 28 days’ notice of termination. The landlord must send the notice of termination to the RTB on the same day it is sent to you. If this is not done the notice of termination will be invalid.

This process for ending a tenancy because of rent arrears is set out in Section 12 of the Residential Tenancies and Valuation Act 2020 .
The RTB has information about this rent arrears process .

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
### Can a landlord and tenant agree a shorter notice period?
You and your landlord can agree a shorter notice period than the minimum periods set out above. But you can only do this when the landlord decides to end your tenancy.
So, for example, if you find somewhere else to live before the termination date on your notice of termination, you should write to your landlord confirming the date you will be leaving. This can help avoid any disputes in the future. You should check the terms of your lease to see if there are any other requirements around ending your tenancy, particularly if you have a fixed-term tenancy .
It is illegal to agree a shorter notice period at the start of the tenancy.
You and your landlord can also agree a longer notice period, but the maximum is 120 days when the tenancy has lasted less than 6 months.

title: If your landlord wants you to leave
text:
## What if I can’t find alternative accommodation?
If your landlord has asked you to leave and you can’t find alternative accommodation, you can contact organisations such as Threshold or Focus Ireland for advice. They can check if your notice of termination is valid and help you with the next steps.
If you are illegally evicted or are unable to leave your rented accommodation after your tenancy has been terminated, you can find information in our page about illegal eviction and overholding .
If you find yourself homeless or you think you may lose your home, you should contact your local authority to access accommodation. There are supports available for people who are homeless and agencies that can help .

14 September 2026
News
Do you rent? From 14 September 2026, certain rental rules are changing .

Not registering a tenancy

text:
# When to register

## On this page

## When must a tenancy be registered?
You must register each tenancy:
When a new tenancy begins: register within one month of the tenancy start date.
Annually: register on the anniversary of the tenancy start date.
You must also update the tenancy registration when there is a change in rent or other tenancy details. For example, if some tenants change but at least one of the original tenants remain.
If the property is sublet , the head-tenant must register the sub-tenancy with the RTB.
You can find detailed instructions about how to register a new tenancy , register a student specific accommodation tenancy , complete your annual registration , or update a registration .
The laws on annual registration changed on 4 April 2022.
You can read more about the system of registration that was in place before this date in ‘The law covering registration’ below.

title: When to register - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Example 1: new tenancy
A tenancy starts on 15 May 2025. The landlord must register it by 14 June 2025 (within one month) to avoid late fees. If the tenancy continues, the landlord must register it again by 14 June 2026, and then by 14 June every year for as long as the tenancy lasts.

### Example 2: existing tenancy
A tenancy started on 9 September 2018. The landlord must have registered it by 9 September 2022 (no later than 8 October 2022) to avoid late fees. If the tenancy continues, the landlord must register it again by 8 October every year for as long as the tenancy lasts.

title: When to register - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Example 3: Further Part 4 tenancy
A tenancy started on 1 January 2016. On 1 January 2020, it became a Further Part 4 tenancy, which could last for 6 years. The landlord registered it on 15 January 2020.
Annual registration started on 4 April 2022. The landlord needed to register the tenancy again within one month of 1 January 2023 (within one month of the anniversary of the tenancy start date, which was by 31 January 2023).
If the tenancy continues, the landlord must register it again by 31 January every year for as long as the tenancy lasts.
There is a temporary fee waiver for Further Part 4 tenancies, if each annual registration is completed on time.

title: When to register - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Registering a sub-tenancy
Subletting happens when a tenant (head-tenant) rents out the property to another person (sub-tenant) while still being responsible to the landlord. The head-tenant must register the sub-tenancy with the RTB.
You must register a sub-tenancy using the RTB1 paper tenancy registration form. You cannot register a sub-tenancy through the RTB’s online tenancy registration system.

## I forget when my tenancy is due for annual registration

title: When to register - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Check your registration account
You are responsible for making sure your tenancies are registered on time. You can check when your tenancy is due for annual registration on your registration account .
Follow these steps:
Log on to your registration account .
Go to the ‘Manage Registrations’ section of the homepage.
Use the filter to select ‘Pending Registration’. This will show you the tenancies that are due for annual registration.
Check the ‘Next Registration Due Date’ column for each tenancy.

title: When to register - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Reminders
We will also remind you when your tenancy is due for annual registration, if your contact information is up to date on your registration  account.
We will send reminder letters by post or email depending on your preference.
First reminder: 30 days before the registration due date.
Second reminder: on the due date, with one more month to register to avoid paying late fees .
Final reminder: 5 days before the deadline is due to expire.
Late fee notice: after the deadline has passed and late fees apply.

## Late registration
You can make your annual registration up to one calendar month after the due date. If you miss the registration deadline, late fees apply for each month the registration is late.

title: When to register - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## The law on registration
Registering your tenancy is required by law under the Residential Tenancies Act 2004 . The legal requirement to register annually is in the Residential Tenancies (Amendment) Act 2019 which came into effect on 4 April 2022.

Other breach of tenant obligations: Landlords can give a tenant 28 days’ notice to end a tenancy where a tenant has breached their obligations. You must have served a warning notice to your tenant correctly first.
Serious anti-social behaviour: Landlords can give a tenant 7-days’ notice to end a tenancy in cases of serious anti-social behaviour or behaviour that threatens the structure of the property. For example, criminal behaviour or threats to safety. You do not need to serve a warning notice first. High standards of proof apply for disputes.

### Ensure your notice is valid
To be valid, a Notice of Termination must:
Be signed by the landlord or their authorised agent.
Include the date the notice is served. This must be the exact day that your tenant receives the notice.
Give the date the tenancy will end (the tenant has the full 24 hours on that day to leave the property).
Give the reason you are ending the tenancy.
Tell the tenant they have 90 days from the date they receive the notice to bring a dispute case to the RTB if they believe the notice is not valid. Where there has been a breach of obligation by the tenant, it should tell the tenant they have just 28 days to bring a dispute case to the RTB.

title: Notice of Termination guide - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Lawful termination or illegal eviction
Ending a tenancy is a normal process, but it must be done legally.
Lawful termination: You must serve a valid Notice of Termination and follow the steps to legally end a tenancy
Illegal eviction: It is illegal to force a tenant out by using threats, cutting off utilities, or changing locks. We take such cases seriously, as they can lead to homelessness.
If a tenant believes they have been illegally evicted, they can bring a dispute case to the RTB. If the RTB finds you have evicted your tenant illegally, we can direct you to allow the tenant to return to the property or pay damages of up to €20,000 (or both).

title: Notice of Termination guide - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Overholding
Overholding is when a tenant stays beyond the notice period. If a tenant stays beyond the notice period, they must continue paying rent.
Accepting rent does not mean you agree to continue the tenancy. The RTB can only order a tenant to leave after a valid Notice of Termination has expired.

title: Notice of Termination guide - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Fixing errors in a Notice of Termination
If there is an error or defect in a Notice of Termination or in how it was served, an adjudicator or Tribunal may allow the error to be corrected, either by:
Using the slip rule: which allows minor mistakes that don’t affect the notice in a significant way to be overlooked.
Allowing a remedial notice of termination to be served: which is a corrected version of the original notice.
These options are only allowed if the mistake:
Does not significantly affect the validity of the original notice, and
The rest of the notice complies with the Residential Tenancies Act 2004 (as amended).
A n adjudicator or Tribunal may also allow t he slip rule or a remedial notice to be used to correct an error in :
A statement or statutory declaration that accompanies a notice of termination.
A nother notification related to the notice of termination , for example, a rent arrears warning letter.

title: Notice of Termination guide - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Rules for serving a remedial notice
If the adjudicator or tribunal allows a remedial notice to be served, the following rules apply:
The remedial notice must be served within 28 days of the RTB issuing the Determination Order.
The notice period in the remedial notice depends on how much time was left in the original notice.
If the original notice period has already expired: The landlord (or tenant) must give at least 28 days’ notice in the remedial notice.
If the original notice period hasn’t yet expired: The landlord (or tenant) must give 28 days’ notice plus any remaining time left on the original notice.

title: Notice of Termination guide - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
#### Example: Slip Rule
A landlord gives notice to two tenants but makes a small typo in one tenant’s first name. The tenants challenge the notice.
The RTB adjudicator decides the error is minor and doesn’t affect the notice in a meaningful way.
The adjudicator applies the slip rule and confirms the notice is still valid. The tenant must vacate.

title: Notice of Termination guide - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
#### Example: Remedial Notice
A landlord serves a notice with 180 days’ notice on 1 December 2024.
The notice period starts the next day, 2 December 2024, so the correct termination date is 31 May 2025.
However, the landlord mistakenly writes 30 May 2025 as the termination date in the notice.
The tenant challenges the notice with the RTB.
The case is heard on 3 May 2025.
The adjudicator rules that the notice is invalid because of the incorrect termination date but allows a remedial notice to be served.
The RTB issues the Determination Order on 7 May 2025.
The landlord serves the remedial notice on 10 May 2025.
Since the original termination date was supposed to be 31 May 2025, there are 22 days left in the original notice period on the day the remedial notice is served.
Therefore, the landlord must give a total of 50 days’ notice (28 days + 22 days).
The new termination date is 30 June 2025.

To legally end a tenancy, you must:

-The property is no longer suitable for the tenant’s needs. For example, it is too small.
-You plan to sell the property within 9 months.
-You or an immediate family member need to live in the property. This only applies to private landlords.
-You plan to carry out substantial refurbishments to the property.
-You plan to change the use of the property, for example to convert it into an office.

## Special cases
Student specific accommodation: Rules for ending a tenancy of unlimited duration don’t apply to student specific accommodation.
Fixed term tenancies: If you have a fixed term tenancy agreement with your tenant, you cannot end the tenancy before the date you agreed unless the tenant has broken the terms of their agreement.

## Notice periods
The minimum notice you need to give depends on how long the tenancy has been in place.
Tenancy length Notice period

text:
## Shorter notice periods
There are some cases where notice periods can be shorter:
Breach of tenant obligations: You must first send them a warning notice that gives them a reasonable time to fix the issue. If the issue is not fixed, you can then serve a Notice of Termination giving the tenant 28 days’ notice to end the tenancy.
Serious anti-social behaviour by the tenant: or behaviour that threatens the structure of the property. You can end the tenancy with 7 days’ notice. You don’t need to serve a warning notice.
Unpaid rent: you can also give a shorter notice period. Follow these steps:
Serve a rent arrears warning notice with the amount they owe and give 28 days to pay.
Send a copy of the rent arrears warning notice to the RTB and to your tenant. The 28-day notice period starts when both the RTB and the tenant receive it.

title: How a landlord can end a tenancy - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Right to return to the property
A tenant must be given the right to return to the property (opportunity to reoccupy) if it becomes available to rent again after the tenancy was ended for any of the following reasons:
Sale of the property: if you end the tenancy to sell the property but no agreement for sale is signed within 9 months of the end of the notice period.
Use by landlord or family: If you or your family lived in the property but you put it up for rent again within 12 months of the end of the notice period.
Change of use: If you changed the use of the property, but you put it up for rent again within 12 months of the end of the notice period.
Refurbishment or renovation: if you ended the tenancy for major works or upgrades but you put it up for rent after the work is completed.

text:
## RTB templates
The best way to be sure the notice is correct is to use the RTB templates. These also include the statutory declaration or statement when needed.

## Serving the Notice of Termination
You must send the Notice of Termination to your tenant and send a copy to the RTB within 7 days. You must ensure that the date of service on your notice is the same day your tenant receives it. Read our Notice of Termination guide for full details.

## After the tenancy ends
If you have followed the above steps correctly, the tenancy will end on the date you set. Once your tenant leaves the property, you must return their deposit quickly. You can only keep some or all of the deposit if there is:
Rent arrears
Unpaid bills and charges (which the tenant was responsible for under the tenancy agreement)
Damage beyond normal wear and tear

title: How a landlord can end a tenancy - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Ending tenancies when selling multiple properties (the ‘Tyrrelstown’ amendment)
If you are selling 10 or more properties in the same development within 6 months, special rules apply under what is known as the ‘Tyrrelstown’ amendment. These rules aim to protect tenants from losing their homes due to large-scale property sales. In these cases, a tenancy cannot be ended simply on the grounds of an intention to sell unless certain conditions are met.

title: How a landlord can end a tenancy - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Conditions for ending a tenancy
You can only end a tenancy in this situation if you can prove that:
The property’s sale price with an existing tenant living in it is more than 20% lower than the market value if sold empty.
Preventing the termination of the tenancy would be unduly onerous or would cause you undue hardship.
You must be able to prove that you meet these conditions to the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB). If a tenant believes you have broken the Tyrrelstown Amendment, they can bring a dispute case to the RTB. An RTB hearing will decide if you have proven that you met the conditions to serve Notices of Termination to sell 10 or more properties under the Tyrrelstown amendment.

title: How a landlord can end a tenancy - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Notice of Termination requirements
If a termination is allowed under the Tyrrelstown amendment:
Each tenant must receive an individual Notice of Termination.
A statutory declaration must accompany each notice, explaining the exemption being used.

## Disputes about ending the tenancy
If there is a dispute about ending the tenancy, either party can contact the RTB dispute resolution service .

# Landlord rights and responsibilities

## On this page

title: Landlord rights and responsibilities - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Who is a landlord?
A landlord is someone who is entitled to receive the rent for a property under a tenancy agreement. The property must be a self-contained residential unit (unless it is student specific accommodation).
A landlord can be, for example:
An individual
A company
A university or private provider of Student Specific Accommodation
An Approved Housing Body (AHB), also called Housing Associations, which are not-for-profit organisations that mainly provide social housing
A trustee of a trust
As a landlord, it is important that you know your rights and responsibilities. Your main rights and responsibilities come from rental law, as well as from any tenancy agreement (written, spoken or implied) between you and your tenant(s). A tenancy agreement cannot take away the rights and responsibilities of a landlord or tenant under rental law.

title: Landlord rights and responsibilities - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Landlord rights
As a landlord, you have the right to:
Set the rent in line with rental law. Rent increases must comply with national rent control rules.
Receive rent in full and on time.
End the tenancy in the first 6 months without reason , unless a fixed-term lease is in place. After 6 months, a tenancy can only be ended for specific legal reasons.
Know who is living in the property and to decide if subletting or assignment is allowed. Subletting or assignment is not allowed in Approved Housing Body or student specific accommodation tenancies.
Be told about necessary repairs and to access the property with reasonable notice to fix them.
Refer disputes to us if the tenancy is legally registered.

title: Landlord rights and responsibilities - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Landlord responsibilities
Landlords must:
Allow the tenant to have peaceful and exclusive occupation of the property, which means you can only enter the property with the tenant’s permission, except in an emergency.
Complete necessary repairs within a reasonable time or refund the tenant for essential repairs they arranged. Expenses must be reasonable and you should get receipts.
Provide suitable bins for rubbish and waste outside the property, where possible.
Insure the structure of the property but tenants should arrange their own contents insurance.
Return the deposit in full as soon as possible at the end of the tenancy, unless you need to make deductions for unpaid rent, bills, or damage beyond normal wear and tear .
Provide tenants with your contact details or for your agent.

We have prepared a handy checklist to help landlords set their tenancy up for success and to avoid future problems. You can view our landlord’s moving-in checklist .

## Resolving disputes

Many disputes can be resolved early with self-resolution through informal discussion with your tenants.

title: Security deposits - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
# Security deposits
A tenant is usually required to pay a security deposit when they agree to rent a property. There are rules on the deposit amount, when it should be paid and how it must be returned at the end of the tenancy.

## On this page

## What is a security deposit?
A security deposit is a sum of money paid by a tenant to a landlord before the tenancy begins.
It is financial protection for the landlord as security to cover any rent arrears, bills owing or damage beyond normal wear and tear at the end of the tenancy.
The deposit must be returned at the end of the tenancy unless deductions are necessary.

## Are there limits on the amount of the deposit?
A landlord cannot ask for a deposit that is more than one month’s rent.
The agreed amount should be documented, and both the tenant and landlord should get a signed and dated receipt.

title: Security deposits - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## When should the deposit be paid?
You should only pay the deposit once you are satisfied with the property and rental terms. Avoid paying in cash (if possible) and always request a receipt.

## Who holds the deposit?
It should be clear at the start of the tenancy who holds the deposit and who is responsible for returning it.
If an agent is managing the property, they may hold the deposit. You must always get the landlord’s contact details.

## When should the deposit be returned?
Your deposit must be returned as soon as possible when the tenancy ends, unless the landlord has a legal reason to keep it.
It does not have to be returned on the day you move out. The landlord may need time to inspect the property.

title: Security deposits - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Reasons for keeping the deposit
A landlord can keep all or part of the deposit for:
Rent arrears : if you owe rent at the end of the tenancy, the landlord can deduct the amount you owe from the deposit.
Unpaid bills: if you have not paid utility bills that you are responsible for under the lease or tenancy agreement, the deposit can be used to cover the unpaid bills.
Damage: above normal wear and tear such as broken windows, holes in walls, leaving the property in an unhygienic or unsafe condition, missing or broken items.
Insufficient notice : if you don’t give the correct notice or end a fixed-term tenancy early, deductions can apply.

title: Security deposits - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
### Holding your belongings against money you owe
Your landlord cannot hold your belongings against money you owe.
The landlord can use our dispute resolution service if they feel your deposit does not cover rent arrears or the cost of damage to the property.

title: Security deposits - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
## Tenant checklist before moving out
Before you move out, make sure:
You provide the required written notice to your landlord.
Rent is fully paid up to your move out date.
Final utility meter readings are taken and payment is arranged (if you are responsible for paying utility bills).
You take all your personal belongings out of the property.
The property is clean so it is in a similar condition to when you moved in, except for normal wear and tear.
You get rid of all rubbish and waste.
Photos are taken at the start and end of the tenancy as proof of its condition.
The inventory is checked to confirm all items listed are present and undamaged.

title: Tenant rights and responsibilities - Residential Tenancies Board
text:
# Tenant rights and responsibilities

## Who is a tenant?
A tenant is someone who is entitled to live in a property under a tenancy agreement in return for paying rent to the landlord. The property must be a self-contained residential unit (unless it is student specific accommodation).
Your main rights and responsibilities as a tenant come from rental law, as well as from any tenancy agreement (written, spoken or implied) between you and your landlord.
While tenancy agreements can cover topics not addressed by the law (such as who pays utility bills), they cannot override tenants’ legal rights.

## Rights of a tenant
You have the right to:
A safe and well-maintained home that is structurally sound, has hot and cold water, adequate heating, and a safe electricity and gas supply. All appliances must be in good working order.
Peaceful and exclusive occupation, which means the landlord can only enter the property with your permission, except in an emergency.
Receive information on how your rent was set, under national rent control rules, your landlord must provide details of the last rent amount set for the property, the date it was last set and how your rent was calculated.
Rent receipts or statements for rent payments and any additional charges paid to the landlord.
Advance notice of rent increases, with at least 90 days’ notice.
Contact details for your landlord or their authorised agent.

## Tenants’ responsibilities
You must:
Pay rent in full and on time even if there is a dispute.
Pay the deposit (if any) and any charges provided for in the lease or tenancy agreement.
Keep the property in good condition and report repairs needed to the landlord.
Allow access for maintenance and inspections with prior agreement.
Inform the landlord in writing of the identity of all occupants (excluding other tenants).
Follow tenancy rules , including verbal or written agreements.
Behave responsibly and not engage in or allow anti-social behaviour.
Give proper notice before moving out.
Avoid affecting the landlord’s insurance by increasing risks.
Not use the property for commercial purposes .
Not alter or improve the property without the landlord’s written consent.
Not assign or sub-let without the landlord’s written consent (AHB or cost rental tenants are not allowed to assign or sub-let)

## If you are in student specific accommodation or renting from an Approved Housing Body
Tenants in student specific accommodation (SSA) or renting from an Approved Housing Body (AHB) have most of the same rights as private tenants. For example, you can access the RTB’s dispute resolution process and your tenancy must be registered with the RTB.
However, there are some differences, learn more about student specific accommodation and Approved Housing Bodies .

## Moving-in checklist
We have prepared a handy checklist to help you set your tenancy up for success and to avoid future problems. You can view our tenant’s moving-in checklist .

## Resolving disputes
Many disputes can be settled through self-resolution with informal discussion. If you cannot resolve the issue on your own, you can refer the issue to us for formal dispute resolution .

Most tenant rights and responsibilities come from the Residential Tenancies Act (2004, as amended).
You can find a consolidated version of the Residential Tenancies Act 2004 on the Law Reform Commission’s website.
